item.title: Belvedere says MCE board needs broad overhaul, not just expertise
item.description: Mayor Sally Wilkinson, Belvedere's MCE representative, wants the 34-member board replaced. "The real question is whether the current board is willing to sack itself."
item.content:encoded:
By TYLER CALLISTER and KEVIN HESSEL

Belvedere has told the Marin civil grand jury it agrees the board governing the region’s public electricity provider is short on expertise and that its members often fail to show up, but it balked at the jury’s prescription for fixing the problem.

The June 16 report found that the board of MCE, the four-county agency once known as Marin Clean Energy that supplies the electricity for most Belvedere residents, had “rarely asserted its responsibility of governance,” while management “appeared to be taking advantage of this situation.” Jurors started digging after the agency’s power costs jumped nearly $200 million in a single year. The day after the report came out, MCE’s longtime chief executive, Dawn Weisz, was gone.

The City Council approved Belvedere’s response unanimously without discussion July 13, agreeing with both findings the jury directed at member cities: that board members have limited expertise for an agency as complex as MCE, and that poor attendance has undercut its oversight. It also agreed with one of the two required recommendations, that cities commit their appointees to attending every board meeting.

Belvedere objected to the second recommendation, the jury’s remedy for the expertise problem: a call for cities to reassess their appointments and pick the members with the most financial and energy expertise. Not every council has such a member, Belvedere wrote, and the recommendation is “at best, an interim measure” that does nothing about the size and structure of a 34-member board.

Mayor Sally Wilkinson, the city’s representative on the MCE board since December 2020, brought the response to the council in a staff report with City Manager Robert Zadnik. Her part in it does not end with Belvedere’s letter. The MCE board on July 16 appointed her to the ad hoc committee of Marin and Contra Costa County officials that will draft the agency’s own reply. Working with staff and a governance attorney, the committee is to bring it to the full board to consider Aug. 20.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Tiburon resident wins fair contest with iPhone shot
item.description: It was Jennifer Isaac's first time entering the county fair. She says she was "shocked, excited, elated, jumping up and down" when she heard.
item.content:encoded:
Jennifer Isaac had already finished her docent-led tour of the Marin County Civic Center when she turned back for one last look — and stopped.

“(I) was just struck by the shapes all over again,” the Tiburon resident says of the building, designed by architect Frank Lloyd Wright.

She pulled out her iPhone, framed the arches from above and captured what she saw. A little routine editing later — converting to black and white, intensifying the contrast, cropping — and she had a photo. What she didn’t know was that she also had the top prize at the Marin County Fair.

The 71-year-old won for her picture, “Marin Civic Center Aspect,” in the cityscapes and architecture class for monochromatic fine photography at the fair, held July 1-5.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: In her photo ‘Marin Civic Center Aspect,’ Jennifer Isaac says she looked to capture the building in a way that would offer ‘something a bit different to say about the Civic Center,’ focusing on its arches from above. (Jennifer Isaac)

item.title: Belvedere’s ‘Toy Story 5’ director reflects on career and what’s ahead
item.description: Belvedere's Andrew Stanton directed "Toy Story 5," which has grossed more than $900 million. He wrote or shaped the story for every earlier film in the series.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time this year, Belvedere resident Andrew Stanton can relax after a stretch that left him, in his own words, “super exhausted.”

He’s on the other side of the country, in New York, spending the summer recharging after two big projects overlapped, along with the extensive travel each demanded.

“Doing the global domination tour at 60 is not as easy as it was when you’re 50,” Stanton says.

The global domination, in this case, was directing a film that has grossed more than $900 million at the box office and counting.

Stanton, 60, is best known as an animator, filmmaker and occasional voice actor. He directed “Toy Story 5,” which reached theaters June 19. It’s his first time directing a film in the franchise, though he has written or contributed the story for every prior installment, beginning with the original “Toy Story” in 1995.

Now vice president of creative at Emeryville-based Pixar Animation Studios, Stanton co-directed “A Bug’s Life” and directed “Finding Nemo” and “WALL-E,” both of which won the Academy Award for best animated feature, in 2003 and 2008. He also directed “Finding Dory,” which grossed $1 billion after its 2016 release.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Belvedere resident Andrew Stanton’s released two feature-length films in 2026: ‘Toy Story 5’ and ‘In the Blink of an Eye,’ the latter of which he’s seen here directing. ‘In the Blink of an Eye’ follows three stories set in three eras: prehistory, the present and a future in space. (via Andrew Stanton)

item.title: Paradise Cove gets A+ for summer and wet-weather water quality
item.description: Only 78% of Marin beaches earned A's or B's this summer, far below the five-year average of 97%. County officials called the drop unusual and want it investigated.
item.content:encoded:
Paradise Cove has again earned an A-plus grade for water quality from a pollution-tracking watchdog, even as Marin’s countywide grades slipped below their usual marks.

The county’s assessment, released by the Environmental Health Services Division on July 15, draws on the 36th annual Beach Report Card from Heal the Bay, an environmental nonprofit that grades pollution levels at more than 650 beaches from Tijuana to Washington using data collected by local agencies.

Some 78% of Marin beaches received A’s or B’s during the summer dry-weather season, the county said, including Paradise Cove, home to Paradise Beach Park in unincorporated Tiburon. Paradise Cove was one of four Marin beaches to earn an A-plus summer grade, along with Horseshoe Cove in Fort Baker, Dillon Beach and central Muir Beach. It was one of just three — with Horseshoe Cove and Dillon Beach — to earn A-plus marks in both summer and wet weather.

The 78% share fell well short of the five-year average of 97% for beaches earning A’s or B’s, a drop county officials called unusual “since lower rainfall is typically associated with better water quality.” The county said the trend warrants further investigation.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Picnickers and pickup soccer players fill the lawn at Paradise Beach Park on July 4, 2024. Paradise Cove again earned an A-plus for water quality in both the summer and wet-weather seasons, one of only three Marin beaches to do so. (Ted McDonnell archive / For The Ark 2024)

item.title: Richardson Bay Sanitary rejects grand jury’s call to consolidate
item.description: District Manager Johnny Tucker says consolidation talk resurfaces every six or eight years. "We don't have time to continually go back and back and back and beat this dead horse."
item.content:encoded:
Richardson Bay Sanitary District officials have rejected every finding and recommendation in a Marin civil grand jury report urging the county’s more than 50 special districts to explore consolidation, with the district’s manager saying the idea has already been studied at length and offers no savings.

The board of directors voted unanimously July 21 to approve the district’s response to the report, “Better Service at Lower Cost — Optimizing Essential Services for the Future of Marin,” released June 11. Named districts are legally required to respond by Sept. 11.

The grand jury found that the fragmented structure of Marin’s special districts creates duplication, uneven fees and service levels, staffing vulnerabilities and weaker long-term resilience across the county.

District officials countered that consolidation had previously been explored and that the report failed to account for districts that have already combined some operations or to recognize the financial challenges a merger would bring.

“By reading this, what I took from it was it was well-written and crafted, it has legs, but if you are a tiny organization that is completely understaffed and doesn’t have good leadership, it has merit,” board President Peter McIntosh said during the meeting. “For our district, I believe it does not have merit.”
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez

item.title: Belvedere backs expansion of shared dock on Strip
item.description: The Beach Road applicants dropped plans for wood platforms on the city-owned Strip after residents objected to private building on the public shoreline.
item.content:encoded:
The owners of two adjoining Beach Road homes in Belvedere may enlarge their shared dock and add two boat lifts — but not the structures they had sought on the city-owned Strip.

The Belvedere Planning Commission voted 4-0 July 21 to allow a 270-square-foot expansion of the existing fixed dock at 310 and 312 Beach Road, along with two new boat lifts and a pair of kayak racks on the city-owned water parcel in Belvedere Cove. The homes are owned by Mark Conroe, at 310, and Scott and Nancy Robertson, at 312. Commissioners Don Schinske and Ghazaleh Jamei were absent, and Isolde Wilson served as an alternate.

The dock is subject to a shared lease with the city that runs through 2039. The commission conditioned its approval on reducing the number of walkway lights on the dock, consistent with a staff recommendation to cut the 35 proposed fixtures to no more than 20, and on using the most open of three kayak-rack designs that Conroe presented.

Senior Planner Samie Malakiman said Conroe and the Robertsons scaled back the request in the days before the hearing, dropping wood platforms and a revocable license for the Strip after residents raised concerns about building on the city-owned shoreline.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Everyday Encounters: A Belvedere resident reflects on pros, cons of growing up in Marin
item.description: He calls the county a weird dichotomy, a place with a countercultural history and, he says, a lot of Connecticut NIMBYs.
item.content:encoded:
Jonathan Evans says he has an atypical view of Marin. Both of his parents were raised in Stinson Beach, in the area’s bohemian counterculture.

“The culture was very out there,” says the 29-year-old Belvedere resident. “A lot of colorful characters. People that were artists.”

His father drove a dump truck, and his mother was a nursing assistant. Evans, who grew up in Corte Madera, says his family’s background was different from the majority of his peers in the Reed Union School District and at Redwood High School.

“It was weird to go to school with a bunch of kids whose parents worked in private equity,” he says.

After high school, Evans sought something different. He and his now-wife left Marin and lived in cities all over the country, including Santa Rosa; Portland, Oregon; Austin; New York; and finally Atlanta, where Evans earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science from Georgia State University.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: Jonathan Evans of Belvedere, whose parents were raised in Stinson Beach, returned to Marin in February after nearly a decade of moving city to city. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Barbara Paula Mogerman
item.description: Barbara Paula Mogerman has died at age 88.
item.content:encoded:
Barbara was born to Mary and George Troutfelt on January 10, 1938, in San Francisco, California. As a small child, she was enrolled in tap dancing school, where she excelled and found great joy. It wasn’t long until Barbara was dancing in her “Shirley Temple curls” to entertain the American soldiers during World War II.

As a preteen, Barbara’s family relocated from San Francisco to Salt Lake City. During her senior year of high school, Barbara met a young medical student, Stanley Neal Mogerman. As a college freshman at the University of Utah, Barbara was reintroduced to Stan at a Hillel party. He soon became the love of her life. At 18 and 23 years old, Barbara and Stan were married.

Two years into their marriage, the young couple moved to San Francisco where Stan began his medical internship at the newly built Kaiser Foundation Hospital on Geary Boulevard. During Stan’s residency at Kaiser, their eldest daughter, Julie, was born. Three years later, Barbara and Stan purchased their first home, an atrium Eichler in Terra Linda where their other two daughters, Diana and then Laura arrived into the world. In 1972, they moved their young family into their dream home in Tiburon.

Barbara and Stan maintained a deep love during their marriage of 58 years, until Stan’s passing in 2014. They enjoyed a full life of traveling, ballroom dancing and spending time with their children, grandchildren, extended family and friends.

Barbara is survived by her daughters: Julie Goldwyn (David), Diana Maureen (Glenn) and Laura LaBouve (Daniel); five grandchildren: Josh Goldwyn, Bryan Goldwyn, Ashley Maureen, Stephanie LaBouve (Zachary), Eric LaBouve and two great-grandchildren.

In lieu of flowers, please send donations to either By the Bay Health in Larkspur, CA (formerly Hospice by the Bay), or the American Alzheimer’s Association.
item.dc:creator: Reader submitted

item.title: Katherine ‘Katy’ Sarah Nixon Mitchell
item.description: Katy Mitchell, born Katherine Sarah Nixon, passed away peacefully on July 16, 2026, at the age of 106.
item.content:encoded:
Katy Mitchell, born Katherine Sarah Nixon, passed away peacefully on July 16, 2026, at the age of 106. She was born in San Francisco to John Stewart Nixon, of Guayaquil, Ecuador, and Clotilde Cabrales, of Sinaloa, Mexico. Katy grew up in San Pablo, San Jose, and Oakland, and spoke fluent English and Spanish.

She graduated from Fremont High School in 1938 and went on to serve in the U.S. Marine Corps, where she was among the first graduating classes of women Marines in World War II. There she met and married a fellow Marine, Ernie Smith, and gave birth to their daughter, Jeanne. The family later moved to the San Francisco Bay Area, but the marriage did not last.

Katy married Bruce Mitchell in 1949 and made her home in Mill Valley, where their son, Tom, was born. After Tom’s tragic passing in 1968, Katy went back to working full-time as a designer and draftsperson of kitchens and homes. In her free time, she and her family and friends built a second home in the Gold Rush town of La Porte, California.

In 1986, Katy moved to Tiburon, where she lived independently, drove her own car, played golf, and gardened. Above all, she cherished time spent with her grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

Katy is survived by her daughter, Jeanne; her son-in-law, Don; her grandchildren Danielle, Paul, and Natalie, and their spouses; and six great-grandchildren, Graham, Whitaker, Olivia, Teddy, Christian, and Cameron, along with other loving family in the United States and El Salvador.

The family is deeply grateful to the caregivers at AlmaVia of San Rafael and By the Bay Health, formerly Hospice by the Bay. In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to Guide Dogs for the Blind.
item.dc:creator: Reader submitted

item.title: Election 2026: Potential challenge is taking shape in Tiburon council race
item.description: The Tiburon council race has its first potential challengers. Parks commissioner Chuck Hornbrook and wealth-management founder Faris Jafar have taken out nomination papers.
item.content:encoded:
The race for three seats on the Tiburon Town Council has drawn its first potential challengers, a parks commissioner and a wealth-management firm founder who have taken out nomination papers for the Nov. 3 ballot.

Chuck Hornbrook, who serves on the town’s Parks, Open Space and Trails Commission, pulled papers July 23, and Faris Jafar followed July 27. Hornbrook is a clean-energy consultant who finished fourth in the 2024 council race and lost a bid for the Reed Union School District board in 2020. Jafar founded the wealth-management firm Jafar Management in 2018 after a career at investment firms including Blackstone, KKR and Citadel. He was passed over for appointment to the Reed Union board in February.

Councilmember Alice Fredericks, first elected in 2001, took out papers July 15 as she potentially seeks a seventh term, and Councilmember Jack Ryan took out papers July 22. None of the four potential candidates have filed or qualified for the ballot.

The third incumbent, Jon Welner, had not taken out papers.

In Belvedere, both incumbents have qualified for the November ballot and face no opposition for two seats. Councilmember Peter Mark qualified July 16, and Councilmember Jane Cooper qualified July 23 after filing her papers July 22. Both were first elected in 2022 and seek second terms, their last under a local custom that limits members to two terms.

Beyond the council races, a newcomer has signaled interest in the contest for the Reed Union School District board. Krupa Antani, a Tiburon resident and Reed Union parent volunteer, took out papers July 24, joining two incumbents and another potential challenger for the three seats.

Candidates must file by 5 p.m. Aug. 7. If any incumbent in a race does not file, potential challengers in that race may continue to file through 5 p.m. 12.

Interested residents may obtain Tiburon council nomination papers from Town Clerk Lea Dilena at 415-435-7377 orldilena@townoftiburon.gov, and Belvedere council papers from City Clerk Beth Haener at 415-435-8913 orclerk@cityofbelvedere.org.

Other peninsula races

Among the roughly 30 peninsula seats on the ballot, the Tamalpais Union High School District board has drawn the most interest, with six residents taking out papers for three seats. Elsewhere, more incumbents have begun taking out and filing papers, though several seats have drawn no interest beyond the sitting members.

item.title: Belvedere eyeing drone rules before deliveries arrive
item.description: The draft ordinance would not touch flight paths, which fall under FAA authority. It targets where drones launch, land and drop off on the ground.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere is weighing a first-in-Marin ordinance to regulate the ground-level side of commercial drone delivery, preparing for a near future in which food and packages arrive by air.

City staff presented the council with a draft that focuses on how and where drones may take off, land and drop packages within city limits. The rules do not restrict overflight or flight paths, which remain under the jurisdiction of the Federal Aviation Administration. Instead, the ordinance targets the local, ground-level impacts of drone delivery that are increasingly drawing attention in the Bay Area.

In a report to the council, staff said the city’s narrow streets, constrained rights of way and limited emergency-access routes make it especially important to act before routine commercial drone delivery takes hold.

Mayor Sally Wilkinson, who helped staff write the ordinance, pressed for action.

“We want something on the books before this comes to life,” she said.

Other councilmembers urged caution. Councilmember Jane Cooper criticized the proposed language, saying it was too vague and could lead drone delivery companies to take advantage of it. Councilmember Pat Carapiet likewise worried that the ordinance lacked specifics in how it would be enforced and tracked. But City Attorney Andrew Shen said the vagueness was intentional, the city’s attempt to keep the law “flexible” as it learns to deal with a new technology and business practice.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: A Wing delivery drone lowers a package on a tether. Alphabet’s Wing announced in March that it plans to bring drone delivery to the Bay Area, and Belvedere is weighing an ordinance to regulate where such deliveries can land and drop off. (Wing Aviation LLC)

item.title: Strawberry Rec picks giant berry
item.description: The district wants public input on colors and design details before finalizing the playground, with GameTime presenting at Community Night Aug. 21.
item.content:encoded:
The recreation district will build a nearly 13,000-square-foot playground centered on a climbable 20-foot-tall berry with two green slides for arms and bouncy footbridges.

The board approved the design and hired playground company GameTime to build it for $2.4 million in a 4-0 vote July 14. Board member Sarah Waterfield was absent.

The district plans to break ground in 2027 on the play area, which it has called a “destination” and a “statement piece” meant to draw families to the recreation center off Belvedere Drive. It will replace Reggie Park, which the district removed in 2023 to make way for pickleball and basketball courts.

The district is also seeking public input. While it says it has decided on the overall design, the board wants feedback on the particulars: minor design elements, shapes and colors. The district will ask GameTime to appear at its annual Community Night event Aug. 21, where the company will present the design and take comments from residents.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: A GameTime rendering shows the proposed playground in context, its climbable 20-foot strawberry and green tube slides set on a patch of grass between the district’s tennis and pickleball courts, foreground, and its baseball field, off Belvedere Drive. A barn play structure sits at left. (GameTime via Strawberry Recreation District)

item.title: Father chronicles daughter’s journey to the Paralympics
item.description: Marin Morrison was diagnosed with a brain tumor as a high school freshman in 2005. She qualified for the Paralympics before dying at age 18 in 2009.
item.content:encoded:
Marin Morrison’s passion for swimming was obvious the first time she entered a pool at age 6, says her father, Matt Morrison.

“It was clear right away that she was … extraordinary for a small child, and she just loved it,” Morrison says.

By the time she turned 13, Marin’s swim times were just 1.5 seconds slower than times that would qualify swimmers for the U.S. Olympic Trials. She even beat 17-year-old Amanda Weir in a 25-yard underwater race in 2003, Sports Illustrated reported in 2009, the year before Weir won two silver medals at the 2004 Athens Olympics.

Morrison says he expected his daughter to improve enough to meet those Olympic-level swimming standards by the time she turned 14, entering her freshman year of high school in the Atlanta suburbs.

“But that’s when … she was diagnosed, and the story became something very different,” he says.

Marin was diagnosed with a brain tumor during her freshman year of high school in 2005. She fought valiantly against the disease, her father says, qualifying for and participating in the 2008 Beijing Paralympics four months before she died at age 18.

Morrison, who grew up in Tiburon, chronicles his daughter’s journey in “Touched: The Marin Morrison Story.”
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Marin Morrison, daughter of Tiburon local Matt Morrison, qualified for the 2008 Beijing Paralympics in September following performances at the U.S. Paralympic Trials that August; she’s pictured at Beijing’s Water Cube, where swimming competitions were held. A promising youth swimmer, Marin Morrison set two national records in her para-swimming classification. She died of brain cancer in January 2009, aged 18. (via Matt Morrison)

item.title: Strawberry Rec rejects grand jury consolidation push
item.description: The district says its mission differs fundamentally from utility and safety agencies, since it runs mostly on user fees, not property taxes.
item.content:encoded:
The Strawberry Recreation District has rejected the core findings and most recommendations of a Marin civil grand jury report that urges the county’s more than 50 special districts to explore consolidation, arguing its role as a fee-supported recreation agency sets it apart from the essential-service providers the report targets.

The grand jury’s “Better Service at Lower Cost” report, released June 11, urges special districts to consolidate to increase efficiency and save taxpayer money. Districts must respond by Sept. 11. Strawberry’s board approved its response in a 4-0 vote July 14, with board member Sarah Waterfield absent.

Most of the report targets the county’s taxpayer-funded utility, infrastructure, emergency response and public safety services, calling for “deliberate, structured optimization.” Strawberry Recreation District says it is a special case. It funds most of its costs through user fees, not taxes, and its facilities and classes are open to the entire public, not just district residents.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Beach Road seawall work is now underway in Belvedere
item.description: Drivers should expect single-lane traffic and sidewalk closures on Beach Road, with the sidewalk near the seawall closed via marked detour.
item.content:encoded:
Work tostabilize the Beach Road seawallis now underway, the start of a monthslong project engineers say is needed to keep the eroding wall from failing in a major earthquake and flooding hundreds of lagoon-area homes.

Pacific Gas and Electric Co. crews began relocating utilities in the roadway on July 17. That project is expected to run through July 29, with possible Saturday work July 25, before the main construction begins. Gordon N. Ball Construction Inc. of Walnut Creek is set to build from July 27 to Oct. 30 under a $3.51 million contract the City Council awarded in April. The work will install steel sheet piles reinforcing about 550 feet of seawall along Beach Road, between the Main Street and Peninsula Road intersections, part of a roughly $4.97 million project.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel
item.media:description: Tow-away no-parking signs line Beach Road, marking the zone where Pacific Gas and Electric Co. crews are relocating utilities ahead of the seawall stabilization project. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Belvedere’s new admin tech finds a career in public service
item.description: Jules Fogarty, 27, is Belvedere's new administrative technician, handling customer service, permitting, records and support for public meetings.
item.content:encoded:
Jules Fogarty’s first years in the workforce were defined by remote work. He graduated from the University of California at Berkeley in 2020, not too long after the pandemic hit, and spent his early career working from home as a data analyst and program manager for nonprofits.

So Fogarty, 27, says he’s happy to now be working at his first in-office job behind the front desk at Belvedere City Hall. He was hired as the city’s administrative technician in April; his responsibilities include customer service, accounts payable and receivable, records management, permitting and support for human resources and public meetings.

“I’m really liking it here,” Fogarty says. “The city’s beautiful, the staff’s really, really nice.”

He says he’s enjoyed getting to know residents and learning the ins and outs of the small community.

“In a bigger city or at the state level or federal level, it’d just be much harder to make relationships with the constituents that you’re serving at the end of the day,” he says.

item.media:description: Jules Fogarty was hired as the city of Belvedere’s administrative technician in April. He serves behind the front desk of City Hall, answering resident questions while also overseeing accounts payable and receivable, records management and permitting and providing support for human resources and public meetings. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: New Business: Hydration Room offers IV therapy, injections for health and wellness
item.description: Treatments range from a $215 hangover IV to a $65 Skinny Shot, plus ongoing GLP-1 weight-loss and testosterone-replacement injections.
item.content:encoded:
Hydration Room founder Dr. Brett Florie was a resident anesthesiologist at the University of Southern California when his wife began suffering from debilitating migraines. Drawing on his growing expertise in the field, he began experimenting with IV treatments for her.

“I put together a concoction intravenously, integrating Western and Eastern medicine, that had a tremendous impact on her life,” he said.

The experiment would later become the foundation for Hydration Room, the IV therapy clinic Florie started in Newport Beach in 2014, which has since expanded to 64 locations across California. The clinic opened itslatest locationat Strawberry Village June 12, taking over a vacant space in the center near Belvedere Drive. The location offers IV-injected vitamins, antioxidants, electrolytes and peptides, among other treatments. Hydration Room joins a slate of other health and wellness shops to come to Strawberry Village in recent years, including Orange­theory Fitness in 2018, Hot Yoga Republic in February 2025 and Club Pilates in June.

The Strawberry Village Hydration Room offers 37 IV and injection treatments with names like “Cold & Flu Remedy,” “Hangover,” “Jet Lag,” “Stress Rescue,” “Skinny Shot” and “Happy Shot.” It also offers ongoing medical injections like GLP-1 weight-loss drugs and testosterone-replacement therapy.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: Registered nurse Johana De Brauwere staffs Hydration Room’s new Strawberry Village clinic, where a row of recliners sits beneath wall-mounted IV bags. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Everyday Encounters: A Pokémon Go player aims to catch ’em all in Tiburon
item.description: Tiburon landmarks like Town Hall and the Old Rail Trail double as in-game PokéStops, giving Cao a reason to explore the town on his lunch breaks.
item.content:encoded:
Denny Cao is tapping his phone screen on a lunch break from his job as a software engineer at Tiburon’s Digital Foundry.

But he’s not checking email or texting. The 29-year-old Fremont resident is trying to defeat an animated monster near the Edward Zelinsky ferry landing in downtown Tiburon.

Cao and two colleagues were playing Pokémon Go downtown on July 8. The augmented-reality game for iPhone and Android devices sends players to real-world landmarks to catch, train and battle the “pocket monsters,” the formal name for the media franchise now featuring 1,028 creatures — and counting. The franchise began with 151 monsters when the original games were released in February 1996 in Japan on the Nintendo Game Boy.

“It just gets you outdoors,” Cao says of the game, which he has played on and off since before its official release in July 2016, when he was a beta tester. He says he was especially grateful for the game during the stay-at-home orders in the early days of the coronavirus pandemic in 2020.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Fremont resident Denny Cao, a software engineer with Tiburon-based Digital Foundry, spent his July 8 lunch break walking around downtown Tiburon playing Pokémon Go, the mobile game that became a cultural phenomenon upon its release July 6, 2016. (Francisco Martinez / The Ark)

item.title: Garden Plot: Names of plants, animals trace back to explorers, naturalists
item.description: Institutions such as the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew and the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh financed many trips around the world to collect specimens that might do well in British gardens.
item.content:encoded:
Both plants and animals are named after people, often those who discovered them, those who played a role in bringing plants to the trade or those who are friends. The British, keen gardeners that they are, were quick to realize the potential of bringing foreign plants to their gardens. Institutions such as the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew and the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh financed many trips around the world to collect specimens that might do well in British gardens.

The Age of Discovery started in the early 1400s, followed by the Enlightenment from the late 1700s into the early 1800s. People became fascinated with finding what else was out there, and seagoing ships were capable of longer voyages. The crowns of Spain, Portugal, France, England and others had financial motivations to discover things like rubber, coffee, spices and other lucrative trade items. These voyages often included naturalists and gardeners who carefully packed barrels of specimens to be sent home for study and cultivation. These trips weren’t without risk, as plant explorers died in the pursuit of more and better plants; David Douglas, for instance, died young after a run-in with a bull while hunting plants in Hawaii.
item.dc:creator: Diane Lynch
item.media:description: Clarkia, a pink native wildflower named for William Clark of the Lewis and Clark expedition, blooms along some of Tiburon’s fire roads each spring. (Diane Lynch / For The Ark)
